1:
The opening verse makes a chronological difficulty all four feel. Ellicott states it plainly: the temple took seven years and the palace thirteen more, and the works were successive, so at face value the verse pushes either the dedication or the divine answer thirteen years past the prayer, the first infinitely improbable and contradicted by Josephus, the second more preposterous. His solution: the notice merely summarizes the three preceding chapters and was never meant to date the vision. Gill reaches the same place through the grammarians: Junius and Tremellius put verses one to nine in a parenthesis and render it for the Lord had appeared, while Piscator begins a distinct narrative, a delay of twelve or thirteen years not being reasonable to suppose. Henry simply repunctuates, reading Solomon finished in the first verse and the Lord had appeared in the second, and dates the vision to the night after the festival. Keil and Delitzsch add that this account summarizes the answer where Chronicles is fuller.

On the hallowing they divide by temperament. Henry presses the prerogative: Solomon dedicated the house but it was God's to hallow, for men cannot make a place holy, though what we sincerely devote he may accept; and he applies it to persons as living temples, whom God sets apart and keeps perpetually in his eye and heart. Keil and Delitzsch locate the sanctifying in a fact rather than a word: Jehovah put his name there by filling the house with the cloud which visibly displayed his presence, consecrating it as the scene of the manifestation of his grace; and the Lord answers the prayer by giving always more than was asked. Ellicott restrains the for ever, holding it determined by the prayer it answers: it marks the temple a settled habitation against the movable tabernacle, and whether it bears a larger sense is expressly made to depend on Israel's faithfulness.

The condition is read as genuinely conditional. Henry takes the entail of the blessing to pass only to those who tread in their parents' steps, and warns that the house was designed to protect allegiance and not rebellion: after all our services we stand on the same terms as before, nothing purchasing liberty to sin. Gill observes that David was guilty of many failings yet never apostatized into idolatry, which is what the integrity chiefly respects, and that the Hebrew runs if in turning ye turn, meaning wholly and not in a single instance. Keil and Delitzsch trace the threat word for word to the Pentateuch, the cutting off from Deuteronomy's curses and the desolation of the house from the curse there pronounced on the land. Ellicott finds the fall of Solomon's house from dominion over all Israel an emphatic comment on how conditional the promise was, the covenant surviving only in an unbroken succession kept for David's sake.

The last clause divides them textually. Ellicott notes that which is not in the Hebrew, so the true meaning is certainly this house shall be high, which the Greek translators read and the Latin glosses as an example; the allusion is to the lofty site, elsewhere a type of glory and here of ruin, since a city set on a hill cannot be hid. Gill offers instead the house of the most High, or high in esteem and fame, on a high hill and a hundred and twenty cubits tall. Henry turns the height into the moral: they prided themselves on the magnificence, but it was not out of reach of judgment, and its height would make its fall the more amazing, passers-by astonished at the ruins as they had been at the fabric. Clarke makes the by-word present tense, the unbelieving and stiff-necked Jew being words still in common use; Ellicott says their continued existence as a proverb through captivity and dispersion is a fact to which world history furnishes no parallel.
10:
The twenty years are the two houses together, seven for the temple and thirteen for the palace, as Gill and Clarke reckon. Ellicott marks a literary seam: the account of building and consecration ends at the ninth verse, and what follows is this notice of Hiram and then brief official records of Solomon's works and government, markedly different in style from the graphic and picturesque passages around them. Keil and Delitzsch find the Hiram notices very imperfect, the fourteenth verse furnishing a conclusion neither in form nor substance, and resolve the grammar by making verses ten and eleven one period, the giving of the cities the apodosis and Hiram's timber a parenthesis. They gloss the address too: my brother is a conventional expression used by princes with one another.

What the twenty cities were is disputed. Henry judges they had not been allotted to any tribe, the border of Asher only coming up to them, but remained with the natives until Solomon mastered them and made a present of them. Ellicott agrees they were probably cities of the subject races, which he would have no scruple in alienating, though the law forbidding the land to be sold for ever would hardly, he adds, have been strictly observed under so self-reliant a despotism. Clarke doubts they were annexed to Tyre at all, thinking Solomon gave only the produce until the loan was repaid, or else that they were heathen cities he had conquered and was free to give; all three note from Chronicles that they came back, were rebuilt, and peopled with Israelites.

Why Hiram was displeased divides them. Ellicott keeps it practical: the discontent probably referred to the condition of the cities, which afterwards had to be rebuilt, not to their position, the western part of that territory lying near the Tyrian frontier and suiting both kings. Henry will have neither party at fault, neither Solomon mean in giving what was not worth acceptance nor Hiram hard to please. The country was valuable but not agreeable to Hiram's genius, the Tyrians being merchants who lived in fine houses and grew rich by navigation and knew not how to value land fit for corn and pasture; a man used to the clean streets of Tyre could not agree with the miry lanes of Cabul, and the best lands have commonly the worst roads through them. He draws the providence out of it: God suits the earth's accommodations to the dispositions of men and the dispositions of men to the earth, so that some delight in husbandry and wonder what pleasure sailors take on a rough sea, while others wonder what pleasure husbandmen take in a dirty country.

The name itself is unsettled. Josephus, both Henry and Ellicott report, did not know it as Hebrew and said expressly that in Phoenician it signifies what is unpleasing. Clarke says the learned are not agreed, notes a Cabul in Asher's boundary, and reports that some therefore read border, as the Greek translators did. Ellicott canvasses Ewald's Hebrew derivation, as nought, and another, like that which vanishes, objecting that unless these answer to something cognate in Tyrian they hardly accord with a passage implying a Phoenician origin; he takes Hiram to play on the one city's name and apply it to the whole territory. On the sixscore talents Gill reads had sent, making it the gold furnished for the temple, five hundred and forty thousand pounds on one authority and nearly a million and a half ducats on another; Clarke makes it the sum Hiram had lent, to repay which Solomon taxed his people, and calls the whole very darkly expressed; Ellicott allows it may be a note referring back, or a payment acknowledging a cession worth more than the debt, and warns that depreciation proves nothing: it is naught, saith the buyer, but when he is gone his way then he boasteth.
15:
Whether the levy was oppressive divides them. Clarke makes it the tax raised to repay Hiram's sixscore talents, grievous as we learn from the elders who came to Rehoboam begging that their yoke be lightened; however plenteous silver and gold were then, he adds, the subjects must have been greatly oppressed by the expenditure. Henry takes the notice as the historian's excuse for the complaint, and defends Solomon twice over: he was a wise builder who counted the cost first and would not begin till he could finish, and he raised the levy not for war, as other princes did, spending the blood of his subjects, but for building, which required only their labour and purses. Ellicott notes the levy fell on Israelites and subject races alike, raised first for the temple and then extended to the other works.

Henry finds the order of the building instructive. God's house came first and was finished before his own was begun, then a house for his wife, then Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, the decayed country cities, the cities of store and chariots, and last Lebanon for pleasure; so let piety begin, profit proceed, and pleasure come last, for if we begin with God he will go on with us, and those consult not their own interest who defer what they design for pious uses. Rebuilding the country towns at his own charge, he observes, made their inhabitants not only his subjects but his tenants, increasing the revenue for his successors; and of Gezer, that Solomon was no warlike prince, but the king of Egypt, who was, took cities for him to build.

Why Pharaoh took Gezer nobody knows. Keil and Delitzsch say nothing is known of the occasion or object, and refuse the conjecture that its people had drawn Egyptian vengeance by a raid on the coast, since by every account Gezer lay not near the sea but very far inland. Gill leaves open whether Pharaoh went provoked of himself or was moved to it by Solomon, who had married his daughter; Clarke recalls that Joshua took the city and it fell to the Levites in Ephraim, but the Canaanites had retaken it and held it until the king of Egypt took it again and gave it in dowry. On Millo they differ in kind: Clarke follows Calmet and makes it a deep valley between the two hills which Solomon filled up and built on, a fortified place for public assemblies; Ellicott works from the word, which seems to mean piling up, so its simplest sense is a fortified mound, notes the house of Millo at Shechem as a hint the word is Canaanitish, and reports that the Greek translators invariably render it the citadel, while Josephus says only that Solomon made David's walls higher and built towers on them.

The sharpest question is whether Tadmor belongs here at all. Clarke says it is almost universally allowed to be Palmyra, and quotes a description ending that the world never saw a more glorious city, the pride of ancient times and the reproach of our own, where the renowned Zenobia and the incomparable Longinus must for ever be remembered with admiration and regret. Keil and Delitzsch note the written text gives the palm-city while the margin requires Tadmor after Chronicles, a form perhaps mere expansion yet still the name the Arabs use, meaning a place fertile in palms. Ellicott alone states the case against: the Hebrew has Tamar, the phrase in the land seems to mean the land of Israel, and the surrounding names are southern, so the place may be the Tamar of Ezekiel or the old name of En-gedi, the margin arising from a mistaken identification. He yields nevertheless to the ancient versions and Josephus, which refer the passage invariably to the famous city, granting that on that reading something has probably dropped out after in the land.
20:
The bondservice is read charitably by one and sharply by another. Henry supposes the remnant had renounced their idolatry and submitted, so Solomon could not in honour destroy them, and were too poor to tax, so he served himself of their labour, observing the law that bondmen should be of the heathen and fulfilling the curse on Canaan. Ellicott thinks the institution was not originated but only enforced and organised, dating in theory from the Conquest, the Gibeonites its notable instance; he traces much of the danger of the stormy age of the Judges to these subject races rising, and compares the whole to medieval serfship, varying in severity by time and region. Clarke is blunter: Solomon put them to the most laborious public works while Israelites were generally exempt, and sets beside it the Egyptian king who built temples throughout his country by captive hands alone and inscribed on each that no native had laboured there, remarking that Solomon might with propriety have put a similar inscription on most of his works.

The Israelite exemption draws the same split. Gill grounds it in law, since they might be hired servants but not bondservants. Henry makes them God's freemen, not bondmen but soldiers and courtiers holding office as qualified, their dignity and liberty preserved and their relation to God as a kingdom of priests honoured. Ellicott doubts it lasted: however it stood in theory it must virtually have been set aside in Solomon's later days, for though they appear here as a dominant race of warriors, princes and officers, like free vassals under a feudal monarchy, the growth of the king's absolute power might remove their condition from serfship more in name than in reality; the subject races could even be played off against them, as the Macedonians were in Alexander's later years when his royalty passed into something like a true Oriental despotism, and later both prophets and history show a serfdom of the poor to the princes. On the five hundred and fifty officers he reconciles the earlier figure, six times as large, by making that the special levy and this a regularly established system.

Why the queen was moved is answered from Chronicles. Gill and Ellicott both give the holiness of the place, the house of David being hallowed by the ark's having stood there, so an Egyptian woman, sometimes in her impurity, was not thought fit to dwell in it; Ellicott ties the notice here instead to the building of Millo, which perhaps trenched on her old quarters. Keil and Delitzsch read both closing notices as pointing back to the third chapter, showing how the incongruities at the reign's opening were removed by the buildings, and explain that she came up because the palace stood on the loftier summit of Zion.

On the three annual offerings they converge. Gill, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch all name the feasts as the passover, pentecost and tabernacles, Gill adding these were by no means the only sacrifices or times, since he offered on sabbaths and new moons as the law commanded, and Keil and Delitzsch that the temple allowed the sacrificing on the high places to end. Ellicott takes the verse for a kind of postscript to the account of the consecration, and states flatly that there is no reason to suppose Solomon on these or any other occasions personally usurped the priest's office. Henry says the same by a different route: with the sacrifices he burnt incense, not himself, for that was Uzziah's crime, but the priest for him and at his charge. He draws the use from the altar being one Solomon built himself: many will assist the devotions of others who neglect their own, and whatever pains we take to support religion we are likely to have the advantage of it ourselves.
26:
Gill and Ellicott agree the harbour's name signifies a giant's backbone, Gill adding that the ridge of rocks before the port lay in that form, covered at high water and standing up in points at low tide. Ellicott turns the name into an argument: it indicates a country which could hardly have supplied shipbuilding timber, so the ships or their materials must have come from Tyre, as Chronicles says. Keil and Delitzsch put it at the gulf's north-eastern end and gloss Eloth as a grove, named from the palms about it. Henry notes the port had belonged to the Edomites and came to Judah only by David's conquest. Clarke reads the number down: the word is literally a ship, and though Chronicles has the plural, it does not appear Solomon built more than one, manned principally by Tyrians.

How Tyrian ships reached the Red Sea exercises Gill, who cannot conceive how they came from the Mediterranean without going far round. He reports that Hiram may have kept a port of his own there, or that the two seas were joined by a river, a notion Lightfoot censured; and he observes this is the first navy we read of. Henry draws the providence from the division of labour, Solomon sending his own servants as factors but hiring Tyrians for sailors who had knowledge of the sea, so that one nation needs another and there may be mutual commerce. Ellicott makes the same fact a point about Israel's vocation. The Tyrians were the great sailors until their own colonists and the Greeks superseded them, but Israel cared little for the sea, its coast was scantily furnished with harbours, and its call to be a separate people was absolutely incompatible with maritime commerce. Solomon's venture was exceptional, with no parallel until the royal houses intermarried under Ahab and Jehoshaphat; and the Old Testament mostly regards the sea for its terrible power, while of the new heaven and earth it is declared with emphasis that there was no more sea.

Where Ophir was nobody agrees. Ellicott alone states what is certain: it lay east of Palestine, was reached by the Red Sea, and its gold became proverbial; all else, he says, is speculation and tradition. Of the three positions, Africa, Arabia and India, he thinks the evidence preponderates for the last two and finally for India: tradition favours it, the Greek translators give the Coptic word for India, the Arabic versions render it India outright, and Josephus says unhesitatingly that Ophir was in his day called the Golden Chersonese. Against this he sets Ophir's place among the sons of Joktan, which clearly indicates Arabia, and the nearness of the queen of Sheba and her gold, holding neither conclusive; gold and precious stones would suit either, while the almug wood is certainly the sandal wood found almost exclusively on one Indian coast, its name a corruption of the Sanscrit.

The others divide. Gill lists the guesses, Ceylon, Sofala, Peru, and the Hispaniola of Columbus, who thought himself that he had found Ophir for its gold, before settling with Josephus on the golden Chersonese, where a mountain near Malacca is still called Ophir. Henry takes it for the East Indies and supposes Ceylon. Clarke says plainly that no man knows to this day, rejects the siting at the two rivers' sources because the voyage took three years, and follows a traveller who put Ophir in Sofala opposite Madagascar, where gold and silver mines have been worked from the remotest antiquity, the monsoons making three years the least possible time. Henry ends on the gold: Canaan, the glory of all lands, had none, which teaches that the hoarding part of this world's wealth is not its best part; Solomon's four hundred and twenty talents were little beside David's hundred thousand, and the merchandise of wisdom, within reach of the poorest, is better than that of silver.
